Champions/Aaron.title: Aaron
Champions/Aaron.content:
A living stream given shape, Aaron moves like a sculpted tide — his form shifting between dolphin-sleek grace and humanoid structure, skin resembling flowing water caught in perpetual motion. Faint ancestral markings pulse along his arms when he channels magic, and water drips upward from his feet, returning to his body as though the sea refuses to let any piece of him go.
As chieftain of Tiderest Shoals, Aaron carries not only the ocean’s memory, but the weight of its future.
The Current That Chose to Move
When the first whisper of the Starfall reached Tiderest Shoals, the waters trembled, and sea creatures fled deeper than the trenches dared allow. Aaron felt the disturbance like a bruise pressed against his spirit — Starfall had touched the land above, and would soon gnaw its way into the sea. He rose from the heart of the Shoals and set out alone to meet the storm before it could meet his people, vowing to return.
In that moment, he thought of Thorall — tide and tundra united once before, and perhaps about to be again.
Abilities (Overview)

Passive — Living Current: Aaron and nearby allies gain increased mana or health regen, doubled briefly whenever he casts an ability.
Q — Against the Tide: A surging wave that damages and slows enemies while granting allies a burst of movement speed.
W — Protection of the Deep: Grants a shield and a temporary Mana Shield to an ally or himself.
E — Unwelcoming Territory: A pulling typhoon that slows and marks enemies; damaging marked enemies grants allies mana or health.
R — Ocean’s Curtain: Empowers nearby allies’ basic attacks and grants Aaron bonus movement speed.

Connections

Tiderest Shoals — his home and the people he leads.
The Shattered Seas — the wider waters he watches over.
Thorall — old friend; tide-and-tundra alliance against the melting world.

Champions/Asterion.title: Asterion
Champions/Asterion.content:
Asterion was born human during the Age of First Civilizations, around 12,000 BCE, and became exceptionally long-lived through unknown astral magic. His obsession with the night sky led him to pioneer astral cartography, identifying the stable star-patterns that influence magic, fate, and natural forces.
He became a founding authority of The Great Concord around 6,000 BCE — but never its ruler, preferring to design systems rather than sit on a throne. During the Concord’s Gilded Age, its influence peaked even as subtle corruption took hold: knowledge hoarding, political manipulation, moral absolutism.
Around 2,500 BCE, Asterion discovered that erased constellations were leaking back into the world and warned the Concord of a cosmic devourer entity. Leadership dismissed his claims, and the order fractured into the philosophical ancestors of Lumia’s preservation-focused sect and Serathiel’s judgment-focused sect. By ~800–50 BCE, Asterion had left the Concord — by pressure or by choice, even he is unclear — and continued his research in secrecy as the Concord became a militarized cabal.
The Starfall
Asterion was in the high vaults of the Meridian Library, finishing a map of the Western Reach, when the Starfall struck. He watched ink lift from his brush as gravity lost its resolve, and the Great Spire shatter into blocks that drifted upward to become the floating debris of The Starfall Crater. He survived by being near the building’s edge, and has returned to the ruins since.
Present Day
Asterion now searches quietly for traces of the cosmic devourer, tracking constellation echoes that have begun manifesting in champions across the world — fragments of lost star-patterns, resonances of constellations that should no longer exist. To him, each champion he encounters is a living clue in an unfolding celestial storm.
Abilities (Overview)

Passive — Celestial Draft: Casting abilities creates Star Points; connecting them forms damaging, slowing Constellation Lines.
Q — Stellar Trace: A line of starlight that damages and leaves Star Points at both ends.
W — Astral Echo: A delayed-detonation zone that leaves a Star Point and can flare connected Constellation Lines.
E — Orbit of Influence: Temporarily expands all active Constellation Lines outward, pulling enemies toward them.
R — Starfall Convergence: A massive zone where falling stars strike along Constellation Lines, collapsing into a final detonation.

Connections

The Great Concord — founding architect.
Celestial Concord HQ — present at its destruction; maintains ties to the ruins.
The Starfall Crater — witnessed its formation.
Lumia and Serathiel — both descend from sects that fractured from his original order.
Krysta, Rhaegor, Varesa, Teostra — each carries a fragment of a lost star-pattern that Asterion has taken note of.

Champions/Bogrund.title: Bogrund
Champions/Bogrund.content:
Bogrund is a mustachioed engineer who treats his mechanized armor and his trusty mace, Bonk, like family. His workshop sits at the edge of the Machine Wastes, where steam, sparks, and the occasional explosion are simply background noise.
When the glow of Starfall shards lit the horizon and Bonk grew restless — eager to march toward the crater and, in Bonk’s own way, punch whatever came out of it — Bogrund grumbled, fixed Bonk’s servos one more time, and went along anyway. “Alright. We’ll go look. But if we die, I’m haunting you.”
Architecture of Preservation
Scavenging in the Wastes for steel his people needed to survive the winter, Bogrund and Bonk found themselves caught between Garvak’s excavation and CR-9’s preservation directive. Watching CR-9’s plating, Bogrund couldn’t help but consider an alternative plan: peel a fin off CR-9 itself while it was distracted. “Or we die. Dying is also an option. Don’t look at me like that, you’re a mace.”
Notable Quotes
“I may be slow, but I’m unstoppable!” · “Step aside, peasants! Science requires… dramatic flair!” · “If it moves, it gets bonked. That’s the law!” · “Oops… did I do that?”
Abilities (Overview)

Passive — Precision Bonk: Every third basic attack deals bonus physical damage, slowing enemies if melee.
Q — Bonkform Toggle: Switches between a heavy melee form (“Big Bonk”) and a ranged form with an Accuracy mechanic (“Long Bonk”).
W — Suit Yourself!: Detaches from his armor for bonus speed and brief invisibility; the empty suit grants nearby allies armor and magic resist.
E — Hook, Line, and Bonker: The suit’s arm drags and suppresses the first enemy hit, then stuns them.
R — Cataclysmic Bonk: Leaps and slams down in a massive impact, automatically re-suiting on landing.

Connections

Machine Wastes — his home and scavenging grounds.
CR-9 — clashed over salvage rights to the ruins.
Garvak — present during the same excavation dispute.
Varesa — exchanges dry banter with him.
Molten Imperium — the civilization whose ruins he scavenges.

Champions/CR-9.title: CR-9
Champions/CR-9.content:
CR-9 is a relic of the Molten Imperium — built, unlike Rhaegor, not as a guardian but as the empire’s forward siege engine, designed to level mountains so its armies could advance. It was constructs like CR-9 that once pounded Thorall’s tundra homeland to ash.
For decades after the Starfall, CR-9 lay dormant in the buried siege vaults beneath the Machine Wastes. When Velrisa shattered the arcane battlefronts elsewhere in the world, the tremor reached those vaults and reactivated CR-9’s internal directive: “Begin bombardment cycle. Continue until nothing stands.”
Architecture of Preservation
CR-9 doesn’t chase kills — it enforces a directive of preservation over the ruins it patrols, treating excavation as a breach. When Bogrund attempted to salvage steel plating from the site for his people, CR-9 moved to stop him, giving Bogrund and Bonk the idea of peeling a fin off CR-9 itself while its attention was elsewhere — a plan as dangerous as it was tempting.
Notable Quotes
“Trajectory locked.” · “Persist… until silence.” · “Molten Imperium sequence reactivated.” · “Your suffering is statistically irrelevant.”
Abilities (Overview)

Passive — Bombardment Directive: Locks onto a damaged enemy and fires a long-range shell at their location after 5 seconds; pauses rather than fires while CC’d.
Q — Pulse Bombardment: A stream of shells fired in a line, slowing each target hit.
W — Ordnance Survey Drone: Deploys a vision drone that drops marker charges, detonating simultaneously on expiry.
E — Concussion Dome: Repeatedly bombards a marked zone, staggering enemies hit enough times.
R — Terminal Analysis: A two-phase ultimate — a telegraphed analysis phase followed by a terrain-altering terminal collapse.

Connections

Molten Imperium — CR-9’s origin as a siege-class relic.
Machine Wastes — where CR-9 patrols.
Rhaegor — a guardian-class relic of the same civilization.
Thorall — his people’s homeland was devastated by constructs like CR-9.
Bogrund — clashed with CR-9 over salvage rights to the ruins.
Velrisa — her actions reactivated CR-9.
Serathiel — finds a machine incapable of sin strangely intriguing.

Champions/Garvak.title: Garvak
Champions/Garvak.content:
Garvak believes that strength alone proves worthiness — “Stand firm. Break worlds.” He measures himself against the world’s other elemental powers without hesitation: “Lava bends. Stone endures,” he tells Rhaegor; “You burn hot. I burn forever,” he tells Teostra; and to Thorall, “Your strength is borrowed. Mine is built.”
Condemned
Serathiel sees none of this as righteousness. To her, Garvak is a war-god worshipper who has judged himself worthy without ever earning it. When Garvak raised his war-cannon toward a village, Serathiel’s golden seals closed around him before he could fire. “I have judged myself worthy,” he laughed. “Then dawn will disagree,” she answered — and a single beam pierced the battlefield.
“Judgment is earned, not claimed,” Serathiel has told him since.
A dent in his plating, oddly mace-shaped, predates any record of Bogrund’s arrival in the Machine Wastes.
Abilities (Overview)

Passive — The Siegeborn: Standing still grants stacking Siege Charges, increasing attack range, ability damage, and resistances; moving removes stacks.
Q — Hellbore Shot: A massive empowered shot from his back cannon, growing in area with Siege Charges.
W — Anchoring Plates: Roots Garvak in place, instantly maxing his Siege Charges, reducing damage taken, and granting nearby allies bonus resistances.
E — Shatter Pulse: A ground slam that knocks back and, while anchored, slows enemies.
R — Earthbreaker Round: Consumes all Siege Charges to fire a massive piercing shot that leaves a burning, slowing trail.

Connections

Serathiel — condemned him for claiming worthiness through strength alone.
Rhaegor, Teostra, Thorall — frequent targets of his rivalry quotes.

Champions/Ka'Ruun.title: Ka'Ruun
Champions/Ka'Ruun.content:
Ka’Ruun is a biomechanical scorpion-titan, bred long ago by an ancient subterranean civilization to shatter cities through flawless ballistic geometry. His crystalline spinal ridges unfold into a living ballista, firing shards that fracture along perfect lines. Where chaos reigns, Ka’Ruun imposes geometry.
Starfire Trajectory
Ka’Ruun found a Starfall shard on a smoldering ridge in the High Sky Regions, in the company of Teostra. The shard pulsed like a star’s heartbeat, and Ka’Ruun — adjusting the dials on his gauntlet after a blast that nearly took the spine off the mountain — declared it had “worked.” Teostra warned him the shard would burn him from the inside. Ka’Ruun’s reply: “That means it worked!” and, grinning, “Then I’ll burn brighter.” He launched himself skyward, laughing like a comet, leaving Teostra to mutter that one day he’d explode — and to smile anyway. “Burn bright.”
Just once, something answered that wasn’t the echo at all.
Abilities (Overview)

Passive — Crystalline Stress / Fracture Geometry: Attacks and abilities apply stacking Stress to a target, reducing their resistances; at 3 stacks the target becomes Fractured, taking bonus damage from Ka’Ruun’s abilities.
Q — Spine Line: A narrow crystal spine fired in a straight line, extending further and applying extra Stress against Fractured targets.
W — Crystal Flense: A fan of shards that slow and apply Stress to enemies hit by two or more.
E — Burrow Beak: A short burrowing dash that knocks up the center target and grants bonus speed against Fractured enemies.
R — Shatter Event: Perfect Intersection: Anchors and charges before firing two massive crystal fault lines; enemies caught at the intersection are rooted and heavily Stressed.

Connections

High Sky Regions and Skybreak Zones — his mobility is best suited to the floating islands here.
Teostra — mentor figure, present when Ka’Ruun found his Starfall shard.
Serathiel — his volatile star-soul reminds her of fallen Concord apprentices.

Champions/Krysta.title: Krysta
Champions/Krysta.content:
Beneath Ashenvale Pyrehold stood the Eternis Core, a colossal living crystal older than any mortal tongue, said to keep calamity at bay by its mere existence. From this giant prism came Krysta — a shard shaped by destiny, forged by pressure, heat, and ancient purpose. She awoke with an oath etched into her being: to protect.
As a child of roughly 12–14 at the time of the Starfall, Krysta was fierce and highly protective, defending her village from Starfall-born monsters at a very young age — behavior that earned her both admiration and resentment. Around 10–15 AD, Varesa began influencing her, posing as a friend, the corruption subtle and psychological. Neither Krysta nor Rhaegor was aware of it.
Soon after, Rhaegor revealed himself to Krysta, believing her proven protection of others marked her as worthy of his Trial Chambers. This triggered her True Awakening: Krysta became the chosen vessel of the Eternis Core, which asserted partial control over her. She now carries three voices — her own, the Core’s (order, preservation, control), and Varesa’s corruption (doubt, unraveling, shadow). No one, not Rhaegor, not the village, not even Krysta herself at first, was aware of the full truth.
The Three Voices

The Crystal (Eternis Core): “Order must be preserved. Sacrifice the few to save the whole. You were carved for compliance.”
The Corruption (Varesa’s shadow): “Let go… let entropy bloom. Freedom in ruin.”
Krysta’s true voice: “For lasting to infinity… sacrifices must be made… even at the cost of some life. Is that true? Is that truly right?”

Every step Krysta takes is a battle not against enemies, but against herself. She sometimes dreams of a world outside the volcano — rain, forests, moonlit lakes — things a crystal should not long for. That desire alone proves she is more than a shard of the Core, and more than Varesa’s spawn.
Abilities (Overview)

Passive — The Crystal of Infinity’s Blessing: Continuously generates Shards that empower her next basic attack with bonus AP on-hit damage.
Q — Shard-nado: A volley of shards toward a target, scaling with and consuming her passive stacks.
W — Rush of Corruption: A brief untargetable glide that ends in a burst of attack speed and movement speed.
E — Piercing Eye: A piercing shard that reveals, slows, and marks enemies for bonus on-hit damage.
R — Truth of Infinity: Throws a massive crystalline core that curses a target; repeated attacks detonate it in a chain of stuns and prismatic damage.

Connections

Ashenvale Pyrehold — her home, and the site of her awakening.
The Eternis Core — the entity that chose her as its vessel.
Rhaegor — guided her toward the trials without knowing the deeper truth; now stands beside her as witness.
Varesa — her corruptor, posing as a friend.

Champions/Lumia.title: Lumia
Champions/Lumia.content:
Lumia descends from the preservation-focused sect that split from The Celestial Concord after Asterion’s warnings went unheeded. Where that sect’s judgment-focused counterpart became Serathiel’s tradition, Lumia’s inheritance is gentler: light used to guide, heal, and shield rather than to deliver verdicts. She remembers the old Concord as “stern elders with unbending gazes” — and chose a different path.
“Judgment without kindness is mere cruelty,” she has said of Serathiel’s order. Serathiel’s reply — that compassion too often blinds — is a disagreement neither has resolved.
(It should be noted — kindness this consistent is rare enough to remark upon, even here.)
A Light for the Lost
Lumia now wanders the Verdant Rupture, drawn to its bioluminescent glow and its lost travelers alike. She has been found kneeling beside dying travelers in the forest, channeling gentle light into their wounds while fireflies gather around her — though even she has heard tremors in that forest that were unmistakably not animal.
Asterion has told her: “You shine with a light the cosmos once cherished. Do not let it dim.”
Abilities (Overview)

Passive — Glitter Glitter!: Affecting an ally or enemy grants stacking Heal & Shield Power for a short time.
Q — Glitter Puff: A cone that blinds enemies and heals allies.
W — Blessing of Butterflies!: Grants an ally enhanced auto-attacks; five stacks ground and slow the target hit.
E — Flourish!: A short dash to an ally that shields both of them, with two charges.
R — Glitter All Around!: An AoE zone that heals allies per second and applies Grievous Wounds to enemies inside.

Connections

The Celestial Concord — her order’s preservation-focused lineage.
Serathiel — philosophical counterpart from the judgment-focused sect.
Verdant Rupture — where she is most often found.
Asterion — has taken note of the constellation echo within her.

Champions/Rhaegor.title: Rhaegor
Champions/Rhaegor.content:
Rhaegor survived the Starfall and remained within his volcano in Ashenvale Pyrehold as the world around him collapsed into the Shattered Age. A relic of the Molten Imperium, the same ancient civilization that built CR-9 as a siege engine, Rhaegor was forged as a guardian of volcanic borders rather than a weapon of conquest.
From early in the Shattered Age, Rhaegor could sense The Eternis Core beneath his mountain through elemental resonance — but he never knew its exact nature, its precise location, or that it had arrived with the Starfall at all. Believing it to be a stabilizing force and a potential safeguard against a second Starfall, he constructed an extensive Trial Chamber Network within the volcano, intended to test resolve, balance, and endurance so that only a worthy protector could reach the Core.
A nearby village survived the Starfall thanks to Rhaegor’s indirect protection. Around 10–15 AD, he revealed himself to Krysta, a child of that village who had spent years defending it from Starfall-born monsters. He believed her proven protectiveness marked her as worthy of the trials — not knowing the Core had already chosen her as its vessel, or that Varesa had begun corrupting her in secret.
Relationship with Krysta
Rhaegor and Krysta are not friends, and not rivals — something in between. He doesn’t fully trust crystals (“they do not bend, they shatter”), but he respects purpose, and the two walk parallel paths toward the same threat: Varesa, and the prospect of a second Starfall. He suspects that one day either the Core or the corruption will consume Krysta entirely. Until then, he stands beside her — not as ally, not as enemy, but as witness.
Abilities (Overview)

Passive — Lava Master: Alternates between Dim and Molten forms; Molten Form empowers basic attacks and seeds Lava Pools.
Q — Molten Smash: Smashes the ground, creating lava pools beneath enemies hit, damaging and slowing them.
W — Searing Core: Absorbs nearby lava pools for a shield; heals while standing on a pool.
E — Eruption Leap: Leaps to a location, carrying lava with him if cast from a pool, resetting Q’s cooldown.
R — Tremors of Devastation: A line of molten force that explodes into a half-circle of lava pools, stunning enemies hit.

Connections

Ashenvale Pyrehold — his domain and the site of the Trial Chambers.
The Eternis Core — sensed but misunderstood for decades.
Krysta — the chosen vessel he believed he was guiding toward the Core.
CR-9 and Machine Wastes — shared origin in the Molten Imperium.
Asterion — observed Rhaegor’s awareness of “a sleeping star” within him.

Champions/Serathiel.title: Serathiel
Champions/Serathiel.content:
Serathiel is a disciplined, immaculate archer descended from The Celestial Concord’s judgment-focused sect — the philosophical inheritance left behind when Asterion’s warnings were dismissed and the order fractured. Where Lumia inherited the Concord’s instinct to preserve and guide, Serathiel inherited its instinct to judge. She fights with a serene, unnerving calm, as though every battle were simply a verdict being delivered on schedule.
“Compassion is admirable… yet too often it blinds,” she has told Lumia. Lumia’s reply — “Judgment without kindness is mere cruelty” — captures the divide between them: two ends of the same spectrum, neither fully wrong.
The Hunt for Varesa
Serathiel considers Varesa an aberration, something that by the Concord’s old doctrines should not exist, and has hunted her before. Their clashes are said to light the horizon in black and gold. “You should not exist,” Serathiel tells her. “And yet — here I stand,” Varesa replies.
Views on Other Champions

CR-9 intrigues her — a machine incapable of sin, and therefore, in her eyes, outside judgment entirely.
Ka’Ruun’s volatile star-soul reminds her of fallen Concord apprentices.
Garvak she despises outright: a war-god worshipper who believes strength alone proves righteousness. “Judgment is earned, not claimed,” she tells him.

The Vigil
Serathiel maintains a vigil at the edge of The Starfall Crater, near the exposed foundations of Celestial Concord HQ. She is convinced something moved in the fog near those foundations, unaligned with the vertical, and refuses to stand down despite Asterion’s belief that she is guarding a memory rather than a threat.
Abilities (Overview)

Passive — Edict of Radiance: Enemies hit by abilities or three consecutive autos become Judged, taking bonus damage and granting Serathiel attack speed and bonus Light Shards on takedown.
Q — Dawnbreak Shot: A narrow beam-arrow that applies Judged and deals increased damage to already-Judged targets.
W — Ritual of Poise: Empowers her next attack into a longer-range, bonus-damage strike that crits Judged targets.
E — Crescent Rivenstep: A crescent sweep that slows, with stronger effects against Judged enemies at max range.
R — Final Dawn: Ascended Verdict: A two-phase ultimate — first marks a target as Condemned and can execute them with a javelin, then ascends into an empowered state with piercing shots and doubled Judged effects.

Connections

The Celestial Concord — her order’s judgment-focused lineage.
Lumia — philosophical counterpart from the preservation-focused sect.
Varesa — hunted as an aberration.
Celestial Concord HQ and The Starfall Crater — site of her ongoing vigil.
Asterion — has tried, unsuccessfully, to convince her to end the vigil.

Champions/Teostra.title: Teostra
Champions/Teostra.content:
Teostra nests along the heated updrafts and volcanic ridges of the High Sky Regions, a dragon-aspected assassin who treats fire as purpose rather than chaos: “It burns only what stands in its way.” She has little patience for Rhaegor’s self-styled title — “Rhaegor calls himself the Lava Warden… but he’s just a smoldering pebble” — and has promised to “melt that smug grin off his molten face” if their paths cross.
The Dragon’s Temper
Sitting atop a smoldering ridge, watching a Starfall shard pulse with cosmic fire in the crater below, Teostra was joined by Ka’Ruun, who skidded to a stop, gauntlet already blazing with starfire he couldn’t fully control. Teostra warned him the shard would burn him from the inside. He grinned and launched himself skyward anyway. “One day, you’ll explode,” she muttered — then, smiling despite herself: “But until then… burn bright.”
Asterion has told her: “The fire within you screams like a dying star. Who lit that flame?”
Abilities (Overview)

Passive — Dragon Flare: Her next attack deals bonus damage based on a target’s missing health and grants her movement speed on hit.
Q — Leap of Dragons: A jump and plunge attack with a smaller “sweet spot” radius dealing bonus damage.
W — Dragon Fire: A line of dragonfire that damages and slows enemies hit.
E — The Fire Within / Reposition: Gains stacking magic penetration from leaps and dashes; while airborne, can dash again using charges.
R — Dragon’s Rage: Empowers all her abilities for a duration, granting infinite mana, reduced cooldowns, faster projectiles, and a full-radius Q sweet spot.

Connections

High Sky Regions — her nesting grounds.
Rhaegor — openly mocks his title and his element.
Ka’Ruun — watches over him, exasperated but fond.
Asterion — has taken note of the constellation echo within her.

Champions/Thorall.title: Thorall
Champions/Thorall.content:
Thorall is a mammoth-like humanoid chieftain from the Frozen Fracture Tundras, leading his herd of warriors, shamans, and the last children of his dwindling people. His homeland endured both the Starfall itself and, long before it, the passage of Molten Imperium siege constructs that pounded the tundra to ash — a history that shapes his straightforward, unyielding bearing.
The Treaty of the Melting World
When Velrisa’s curse began destabilizing the glaciers, Thorall met Aaron on the Great Shelf — a tongue of ice groaning under a rising sea. The melt threatened Aaron’s reefs as much as Thorall’s home; rather than let one disaster create another, the two struck a bargain: Thorall’s mammoths would haul resonance-stones so Aaron could use his “Ocean’s Curtain” ability to draw the heat away, breaking the mountain together rather than letting either side drown or be buried. The bond between them — “tide and tundra united” — has held ever since.
“Velrisa’s curse will not conquer us!” Thorall has sworn.
The Mammoth’s Burden
As Starfall fragments destabilized the tundra further, Thorall marched his herd toward the breach with his people in tow, reassuring a frightened child that “no force can break us if we remain together.” But as they neared the crater, the ground rumbled — and something enormous awoke beneath the ice.
Asterion has told him: “An ancient constellation clings to your spirit. Even the heavens remember your strength.”
Abilities (Overview)

Passive — The Blood of Leviathans: Gaining a shield grants health regen and bonus resistances for its duration; a portion of any remaining shield converts to health when it expires.
Q — Let My Presence Be Known: A forward dash that damages enemies, knocking them up if Thorall is shielded.
W — Blood for Glory: Sacrifices a percentage of his max health for a shield.
E — Call of the Mammoth / Mammoth’s Wrath: A two-cast AoE — first an AP roar that empowers his attacks and grants shields on hit, then a slash dealing damage based on his current shields.
R — Thorall’s Hoard: Summons a herd of mammoths to trample a line, slowing enemies and shielding Thorall and his allies.

Connections

Frozen Fracture Tundras — his homeland.
Aaron — old friend; tide-and-tundra alliance against the melting world.
Molten Imperium — historical aggressor against his people.
Velrisa — her curse destabilized his homeland’s glaciers.
Asterion — has taken note of the constellation echo within him.

Champions/Varesa.title: Varesa
Champions/Varesa.content:
Varesa was once a marksman blessed by twilight — a sniper of renown who struck from distances unseen. When death came for her, she stepped willingly into the void between worlds, and returned carrying the shadows themselves. Cold, deliberate, and soft-spoken, she speaks as though every word echoes from another realm. Her arrows are whispers of forgotten souls; her laughter, rare and distant, sounds like steel drawn across silk.
She is calculated and patient — a true hunter in the dark, finding beauty in decay and silence. She fights like a poet of shadows: every strike deliberate, every retreat premeditated. She hunts primarily within the lightless forests of the Starfall Shard Zones.
The Corruption of Krysta
Around 10–15 AD, Varesa began influencing Krysta, posing as a friend. The corruption was subtle and psychological — neither Krysta nor Rhaegor was aware of it at the time. After Krysta’s True Awakening as vessel of The Eternis Core, Varesa’s influence became one of the three voices in Krysta’s mind: a whisper of doubt, unraveling, and shadow, set against the Core’s order and Krysta’s own resolve.
Hunted by the Concord
Serathiel, last loyal adjudicator of the Celestial Concord’s judgment-focused sect, considers Varesa an aberration — something that, by the Concord’s old doctrines, should not exist. Serathiel has hunted her before, and their battles are said to light the horizon in black and gold. “You should not exist,” Serathiel tells her. “And yet — here I stand,” Varesa replies.
Abilities (Overview)

Passive — Shadows Within: Every attack fires an additional mini shadow arrow for bonus physical damage; critical strikes fire two.
Q — Rain of Shadows: An arrow that duplicates on impact, raining darkness in an area and slowing enemies.
W — Dark Frenzy: A burst of attack speed during which her shadow arrows cause bleeding.
E — Shadows Rising / Reap: Builds Darkness stacks from combat; can transform her bow into a scythe that deals missing-health damage and grants permanent AD on kill.
R — Through Worlds: Becomes a living shadow, gaining movement speed and untargetability, but cannot attack or use abilities.

Connections

Krysta — her corruption is one of the three voices in Krysta’s mind.
Rhaegor — encountered Krysta alongside him during her True Awakening.
Serathiel — actively hunts her as a remnant of the Concord’s old judgment doctrines gone wrong.
Starfall Shard Zones — hunts within the lightless forest belt.

Champions/Velrisa.title: Velrisa
Champions/Velrisa.content:
Velrisa was once something gentler. The whispers that found her in the dark — “You used to heal. You begged for peace. But look how they cast you aside…” — preyed on the memory of a time when restraint cost lives. A second voice, her own, answered: “Ignite them. Heal yourself.”
Embers of Sanity
Alone with a candle that danced unnaturally, stretched thin as if trying to escape its wick, Velrisa crushed it in her fist. Hot wax burned her palm, and something inside her laughed. Fire flickered from her fingertips; her eyes glowed violet, and the room lit with spectral embers — her sanity cracking like porcelain. “I will soothe nothing. Tonight, I set the world free.”
Asterion later told her: “The sky unmade the pattern you wield… yet here it stands again.”
Shattering the Battlefronts
Velrisa’s unraveling sent shockwaves through the world’s remaining arcane infrastructure. The tremor reached the buried siege vaults beneath the Machine Wastes, reactivating long-dormant Molten Imperium constructs — including CR-9, which woke not from malice, but because its directive simply re-ignited.
Abilities (Overview)

Passive — Dark Influence: A dark aura grants nearby allies bonus damage, attack speed, and movement speed (the latter scaling with their missing health).
Q — Cursed Touch: Imbues an ally’s basic attacks with bonus magic damage that slows and weakens enemies hit.
W — Unholy Exhilaration: Curses an ally with massive movement and attack speed at the cost of armor and magic resist, extendable by their own attacks.
E — Abyssal Zone: A corrupted area that damages enemies over time and shreds their resistances.
R — Symphony of Ruin: Nearsights enemies in a huge radius, amplifies Unholy Exhilaration on all allies, and empowers the surrounding Abyssal Zone.

Connections

Molten Imperium and CR-9 — her shattering of the arcane battlefronts reactivated their dormant machines.
Machine Wastes — site of the reactivated siege vaults.
Asterion — has taken note of the constellation echo within her.

Characters/The-Archivist-of-Starwatch-Ke.title: Compiler of the Starfall Anthology, resident of [[Starwatch Keep]]
Characters/The-Archivist-of-Starwatch-Ke.content:
Every compiled history of the Starfall and the eras before and after it — the Anthology of short accounts from across the world, the long chronological history of the unnamed world — carries the same byline: Compiled by the Archivist of Starwatch Keep. Beyond that, almost nothing is confirmed. No account describes the Archivist directly; they exist only as the voice arranging everyone else’s stories into order.
The scope and accuracy of the compiled histories suggest someone with access to records spanning millennia, and the patience to organize them — qualities that have led some to quietly wonder whether the Archivist might be Asterion himself, working under a different name from Starwatch Keep. Asterion has never confirmed or denied this, and continues his own research “in secrecy” by his own account, which neither proves nor disproves the theory.
Stranger still: in all the centuries these records have circulated, no one has ever produced a firsthand account of visiting Starwatch Keep or meeting the Archivist in person. The records simply arrive, complete and current, wherever they’re needed, and entries describing events thousands of years apart, from the founding of The Great Concord to the present day, are written in the same hand, the same dry tone, without so much as a shift in phrasing to mark the passage of time. Either something has been writing, uninterrupted, since before the Starfall, or “the Archivist” has never been one person at all.
Connections

Starwatch Keep — the Archivist’s home and library.
Asterion — a possible, unconfirmed identity for the Archivist.

Characters/The-Cosmic-Devourer.title: The entity [[Asterion]] warned [[The Celestial Concord]] about
Characters/The-Cosmic-Devourer.content:
Around 2,500 BCE, Asterion noticed that certain constellations were vanishing from the night sky — not fading, but erased outright, as though something had reached into the Pattern itself and removed them. He warned The Celestial Concord that whatever was responsible, a cosmic devourer, was beginning to leak its presence back into the world.
The Concord’s leadership dismissed the warning. In hindsight, that dismissal may have cost them everything: the order fractured shortly after into the sects that became Lumia’s and Serathiel’s traditions, and Asterion’s claim went uninvestigated for over two thousand years.
Whether the Cosmic Devourer caused the Starfall, was freed by it, or is entirely unrelated remains unknown. What is known is that since the Starfall, fragments of those erased constellations have begun resurfacing as echoes within certain champions — exactly the kind of leakage Asterion warned about, two and a half millennia later.
If the Cosmic Devourer exists, no one currently knows where it is, what it wants, or whether the Starfall was its arrival, its escape, or merely its first breath.
Cross-referenced against Asterion’s personal charts.
And if you’re reading this — it already knows.
Connections

Asterion — first identified it, and still searches for it.
Constellation Lines & Star Points — the discipline through which its traces are tracked.
The Celestial Concord — dismissed the original warning.

Factions-and-Organisations/Post-Starfall.title: Factions and ideologies that formed around [[Starfall Fragments]]
Factions-and-Organisations/Post-Starfall.content:
As Starfall Fragments began surfacing across the world from roughly 3–10 AD, new factions and ideologies formed around them — some treating fragments as weapons, some as energy sources, and some as objects of religious or ideological significance. No global empire has unified the world since the fall of The Great Concord; instead, the political landscape is a patchwork of city-states, nomadic confederations, fragment cult territories, and hidden enclaves.
Borders between these territories are fuzzy, dangerous, and actively contested, especially near the Starfall Shard Zones where fragments are most plentiful. Maps of the region tend to mark such areas simply as “unstable zones” or worse.
Connections

Starfall Fragments — the basis of these factions’ power and belief.
Starfall Shard Zones — where fragment cult territories are most concentrated.
The Great Concord — the last global institution, whose fall left this vacuum.

Note
This account is compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.

Factions-and-Organisations/Post-Starfall.title: The Verdant Wardens
Factions-and-Organisations/Post-Starfall.content:
The Verdant Wardens are not an organization in any administrative sense. They have no leader, no hierarchy, no membership process, and no formal doctrine. What they have is a practice: moving through the Verdant Rupture, maintaining trail markers, guiding travelers who have become lost, and managing — as best they can — the things that grow in the Rupture’s deeper zones that were not there before the Starfall.
New Wardens find the practice rather than being recruited to it. Someone survives the Rupture when they shouldn’t have, and encounters a Warden in the process, and the Warden teaches them what they know, and eventually the survivor becomes a Warden themselves. The knowledge transfers person to person, with no institution behind it.
The Script
The Wardens keep records in a script that no outside scholar has been able to identify. It is not a cipher of any known writing system. It appears to have its own grammar. Wardens who are asked where the script came from say, without apparent awareness that this is strange, that it is simply how records are kept — that they learned it the same way they learned everything else, from the Warden who taught them.
Lumia has seen the script. She did not recognize it. She did not comment on this to the Warden who showed her, because she did not want to alarm them. She has thought about it since. The script is consistent with notational systems used in pre-Starfall naturalistic magic traditions on the eastern continent — specifically traditions that predate anything she was taught.
The Wardens are, without knowing it, writing in the language of the Verdant Dominion. How this knowledge passed through sixty years of post-Starfall chaos, person to person, without anyone knowing what it was, is not explained by anything currently understood.
The Rupture’s Interior
The Wardens do not go to the center of the Rupture. This is not a rule — it is a shared understanding, arrived at independently by every Warden who has been practicing long enough. The outer zones of the Rupture are navigable with knowledge. The inner zones are navigable with luck. The center has not been mapped because no Warden who has moved toward it has returned to report what they found there.
What the center contains — the Green Seat, the Dominion’s capital, the organism that Lumia described as “not an animal” — is not formally acknowledged by the Wardens as a subject of study. They know something is there. They have decided, collectively and silently, that knowing more than this would not help anyone.
Lumia
Lumia operates in the Rupture but is not a Warden. The Wardens are aware of her, respect her, and are slightly unnerved by her — not because she is dangerous, but because she goes places in the Rupture that Wardens don’t go, and emerges without apparent difficulty. She has never asked them about the script. They have never asked her what she finds at the edges of the inner zone.
The relationship is cordial and mutually avoidant on every subject that matters.
Connections

Verdant Rupture — the Wardens’ territory.
The Verdant Dominion — the civilization whose script and methodology the Wardens unknowingly carry.
Lumia — operates in the same territory; parallel rather than collaborative.
Fragment Cults — some cult factions have attempted to establish presence in the Rupture’s outer zones. The Wardens discourage this quietly. If discouragement fails, the Rupture itself tends to handle it.

Compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.

Factions-and-Organisations/Pre-Starfall/.title: Molten Imperium
Factions-and-Organisations/Pre-Starfall/.content:
The Molten Imperium was the dominant military-industrial power of the eastern continent for over seven thousand years. It did not conquer for wealth or glory — it conquered because it believed it was supposed to. Its founders claimed descent from the volcanic peoples of the western continent, specifically the region now called Ashenvale Pyrehold, and with that claim came a doctrine: that Rhaegor himself had charged their bloodline with the unification of the world. There is no record of Rhaegor making any such charge. There is no evidence the founding lineage ever set foot in Ashenvale. Neither fact slowed the Imperium’s expansion by a single year.
The claim may have been fabricated. It may have been sincere. The Imperium’s own records, most of which were buried under The Ashen Seat when the eastern continent’s arcane infrastructure collapsed at Year 0, do not settle the question. What survives are the constructs — and constructs do not record reasons, only directives.
Structure and Expansion
The Imperium was built on two things: volcanic energy harvested from the eastern continent’s interior ranges, and construct-labor that never tired, never demanded wages, and never questioned orders. Its cities were industrial in a way no other civilization of the era matched — smoke, heat, and the rhythmic sound of forges running without pause.
Expansion moved southward across the eastern continent over millennia, into the territories of the Tundra Confederation — Thorall’s ancestors. The Confederation had no constructs, no siege engines, and no unified military. What they had was terrain and the willingness to retreat. They retreated until the ice gave them nowhere left to go. The constructs CR-9’s kind built were not designed to exterminate — they were designed to advance, to level terrain for roads and supply lines. The destruction of the Confederation’s homeland was, to the Imperium’s administrators, a logistical side effect.
Rhaegor
The Imperium’s relationship with Rhaegor is the central contradiction of its history. They claimed his authority as the foundation of their mandate. They built constructs in his image. They named their guardian-class constructs Wardens, after the role they believed he held. And Rhaegor, in his volcano on the western continent, appears to have been entirely unaware of them — or chose to be.
Whether he knew and said nothing, or simply never knew the Imperium existed, is not recorded anywhere. Notes on this period are unusually sparse.
(The notes from this period were revised. I am not certain the current version is what I first wrote.)
Collapse
The Imperium did not fall in the Starfall — it fell because of it. The impact on the western continent severed the arcane relay network that the Imperium had quietly tapped into over the centuries. Without the relay, the construct-control infrastructure went dark. Siege vaults sealed themselves on emergency protocol. The cities, built to run on construct-labor and volcanic-tap energy, could not maintain themselves without either.
What remained became the Machine Wastes: half-buried mega-cities, sealed vaults, autonomous constructs running on emergency directives with no one left to update them.
Legacy
Confirmed relics:

CR-9 — a siege-class construct, reactivated in ~22 AD when Velrisa’s shattering of the arcane battlefronts sent tremors through the sealed vaults.

Another legacy is less tangible: the Imperium’s founding myth — the Ashenvale bloodline, the Rhaegor mandate, the doctrine of unification — survived in fragments through oral tradition, and portions of it were absorbed into at least one post-Starfall Fragment Cult. The Cult does not know where the doctrine came from. It does not ask.
Connections

Rhaegor — guardian-class relic; the Imperium’s claimed patron, who has never confirmed the claim.
CR-9 — siege-class relic; still active.
Machine Wastes — the Imperium’s collapsed heartland.
The Ashen Seat — the Imperium’s buried capital.
Ashenvale Pyrehold — the ancestral homeland the Imperium’s founders claimed. Whether truthfully is unknown.
Tundra Confederation — the civilization the Imperium’s expansion destroyed.
Thorall — last known chieftain of the Confederation’s surviving remnant.
Fragment Cults — at least one sect carries distorted fragments of Imperium doctrine without knowing the source.

Compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.

Factions-and-Organisations/Pre-Starfall/.title: The Ashenvale Clans
Factions-and-Organisations/Pre-Starfall/.content:
The Ashenvale Clans are not a civilization in any formal sense — they are a loose category for the tribal cultures that have lived in the shadow of Rhaegor’s Peak for as long as anyone has recorded anything on the western continent. They had no shared government, no shared language in its entirety, and no collective name for themselves. The name “Ashenvale Clans” is a Concord-era administrative label, invented by scholars who needed something to write in their registers.
What the clans shared was the mountain. Every clan in the region oriented itself around Rhaegor’s Peak — either toward it, as a sacred site, or away from it, as a boundary marker, or against it, as a challenge. No clan ignored it. The mountain did not permit neutrality.
Rhaegor
The clans’ relationship with Rhaegor varied enormously. Some treated him as a god. Some treated him as a natural phenomenon that occasionally moved. Some had no mythology about him at all — only a practical understanding that the mountain’s guardian existed, that disturbing him was inadvisable, and that proximity to his domain made certain things easier (warmth, ore, protection from outside raiders) and certain things harder (everything else).
The clans that treated Rhaegor as a god developed elaborate liturgies around the idea that they were his chosen people, that his protection of their region was intentional and personal, and that correct ritual observance would earn continued protection. Rhaegor has never confirmed this interpretation. He has also never corrected it, which the liturgists consider evidence in their favor.
Whether the Molten Imperium’s founding bloodline genuinely descended from an Ashenvale clan — as it claimed — is a question the clans themselves cannot answer, because no clan maintained records that go back far enough. The claim is detailed enough to be suspicious and vague enough to be unfalsifiable. Rhaegor, who would know, has not commented.
(There is one Concord-era field survey of the Ashenvale region, dated ~3,800 BCE, that was removed from the standard archive. I have not been able to locate it.)
The Starfall
The Ashenvale region survived the Starfall better than almost anywhere else on the western continent. The volcanic geography absorbed and deflected significant impact energy. Rhaegor’s active management of the mountain’s response — if he actively managed it, which is assumed but not documented — may have prevented a larger catastrophe for the surrounding area.
The clans that survived the Starfall in the region coalesced over the following decades into the informal network of settlements now called Ashenvale Pyrehold. Cinderhearth is the largest and most organized of these — a genuine village rather than a camp, with structures built to last and a population that has begun to think generationally rather than seasonally.
The older clan distinctions — which mountain-face a clan lived on, which ritual calendar they followed, which interpretation of Rhaegor they held — are fading. The survivors are becoming simply the people of Ashenvale, which would have been meaningless to their grandparents and feels inevitable to their children.
What Persists
The memory of the clans’ varied Rhaegor mythologies persists in fragments, passed between elders who remember their parents’ versions. At least three mutually contradictory origin stories for the mountain exist among Cinderhearth’s current population. Nobody fights about them. After the Starfall, the question of whether Rhaegor chose them feels less urgent than the question of whether they will survive the winter.
One tradition, held by a small number of Cinderhearth’s oldest residents, holds that the mountain has a heart — a crystal that glows beneath the rock, older than the clans, older than Rhaegor, older than the volcano itself. They do not know what it is or what it does. They know that their grandparents’ grandparents spoke of it, and that the mountain occasionally hums at a frequency that has no other explanation.
Krysta grew up hearing this tradition. She did not believe it until she had reason to.
Connections

Rhaegor’s Peak — the geographical and mythological center of clan identity.
Rhaegor — the mountain’s guardian; variously interpreted by different clans.
Ashenvale Pyrehold — the post-Starfall successor region.
Cinderhearth — the largest surviving settlement; effectively the Clans’ living remnant.
Krysta — grew up in Cinderhearth; carries traces of clan tradition about the mountain’s heart.
Molten Imperium — claimed descent from the Ashenvale Clans. The Clans’ own records do not confirm or deny this.
The Eternis Core — the crystal the oldest clan traditions spoke of. Now confirmed to exist.

Compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.

Factions-and-Organisations/Pre-Starfall/.title: The lost order of astral scholars founded by [[Asterion]]
Factions-and-Organisations/Pre-Starfall/.content:
The Celestial Concord began as a transnational scholarly order dedicated to cataloging and safeguarding astral knowledge, founded around 6,000 BCE with Asterion as a founding authority. Its capital, The Great Concord, and its seat of power, Celestial Concord HQ, grew into the most advanced institution of the pre-Starfall world.
At its height during the Gilded Age, the Concord acted as arbitrator between nations and keeper of magical law, developing star-powered enforcement divisions and institutionalizing astral magic. With that power came subtle corruption: knowledge hoarding, political manipulation, and moral absolutism.
The Fracture
Around 2,500 BCE, after Asterion’s warnings of a “cosmic devourer” were dismissed, the order split into two philosophical sects:

A preservation-focused sect, ancestor to Lumia’s tradition.
A judgment-focused sect, ancestor to Serathiel’s order.

By the time of the Starfall, the Concord had become a militarized, dogmatic cabal. The Starfall destroyed it outright — most of its leadership died instantly, and its magically linked structures lost their connections forever.
Legacy
No global institution has replaced the Concord since. Its two philosophical descendants, Lumia and Serathiel, operate independently and often at odds. Varesa is hunted by Serathiel’s order as a remnant of the Concord’s old judgment doctrines gone wrong.
Connections

Asterion — founding authority.
The Great Concord — the Concord’s capital city.
Celestial Concord HQ — the Concord’s seat of power.
Lumia and Serathiel — inheritors of its fractured philosophy.
Varesa — hunted as an aberration of its old doctrines.

Note
Compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.

Factions-and-Organisations/Pre-Starfall/.title: The Coastal Leagues
Factions-and-Organisations/Pre-Starfall/.content:
The Coastal Leagues were never a nation. They were a compact between maritime city-states along the western continent’s coast — a shared framework for trade, navigation rights, and the resolution of disputes between cities that were too interdependent to war with each other and too proud to formally unify. The league seat rotated between member cities on a fixed cycle, ensuring no single city held permanent authority. This worked because none of them trusted each other enough to let it fail.
Their power came from the sea crossing. Before reliable star-navigation existed, the passage between the western and eastern continents was a matter of luck as much as skill — long enough that a miscalculation meant death, unpredictable enough that even experienced captains lost ships. The cities that controlled the western departure points controlled access to the crossing, which meant access to the eastern continent’s resources, which meant everything.
Asterion and the Star-Charts
The Leagues’ transformation from prosperous but precarious maritime trading cities into the dominant political force of the western continent’s coast traces directly to Asterion. He was not a sailor and had no particular interest in trade. He was interested in the sky, and the sky over open water was cleaner than the sky over any city he had lived in.
He spent time in the coastal cities in the period around 8,000–7,000 BCE, mapping star positions with a precision no one had previously achieved. The captains who saw his charts recognized immediately what they were worth. The city councils recognized it slightly later. By the time the Leagues formally commissioned a dedicated observatory — the first institutional structure Asterion had ever been attached to — they had already been using his methodology for two generations.
The observatories became schools. The schools trained navigators, then cartographers, then natural philosophers who found Asterion’s framework applicable to questions that had nothing to do with ocean crossings. The Leagues funded this expansion not out of intellectual generosity but because the more things Asterion’s methods could do, the more valuable the cities that employed those methods became.
This is the seed of what eventually became the Celestial Concord. The Concord did not emerge from a single visionary institution — it emerged from decades of correspondence between people trained in similar methods across multiple cities on two continents, slowly developing shared vocabulary, then shared standards, then a shared name. The Leagues were the first major patron and the most commercially minded. They shaped the Concord’s early pragmatism.
The Inner Sea
Before the Starfall, the body of water between the two continents was called the Inner Sea by the western coastal cities — the sea between the known worlds, navigable by those with skill and charts. It was not calm or safe, but it was understood. The League cities maintained relay stations on the larger mid-sea islands, which served as waypoints for the crossing.
The Starfall fractured the seabed and reconfigured the sea entirely. The relay stations were destroyed or submerged. The island waypoints shifted or sank. The crossing, already difficult, became actively hostile. The League cities that survived the impact were no longer the gatekeepers of a known route — they were the survivors of a coast that had been rebuilt into something unfamiliar.
The Shattered Seas is what the Inner Sea became.
Collapse and Succession
Most of the League’s major cities were on the coast facing the World Scar’s direction of impact. The seismic and tidal consequences destroyed the majority within hours. A few inland-situated members survived as rump settlements — no longer coastal, no longer trading cities, no longer part of any league, but alive.
Some of these successor settlements still exist in the current era as anonymous villages with unusually good astronomical traditions, and navigators who know star-positions by instinct without knowing why. The knowledge descended without the institution that created it.
One of these villages, somewhere on the western continent’s coast, maintains astronomical records that predate the Starfall by several centuries — kept in a format consistent with early cartographic notation, updated continuously to the present day. The village has no name in any current register. It does not appear on any map made after Year 0.
Connections

Asterion — the Leagues’ most consequential patron; the relationship was mutual but never personal.
The Celestial Concord — the institution that grew from the Leagues’ observatories.
The Shattered Seas — what the Inner Sea became after the Starfall.
The World Scar — the impact’s direction destroyed most of the League’s coastal cities.

Compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.

Factions-and-Organisations/Pre-Starfall/.title: Tundra Confederation
Factions-and-Organisations/Pre-Starfall/.content:
The Tundra Confederation was not built. It accumulated — clan by clan, generation by generation, across the frozen south of the eastern continent, in the territory now called the Frozen Fracture Tundras. It had no capital, no written law, and no permanent administrative structure. What it had was the assembly: every few seasons, representatives from each clan would travel to a designated meeting ground — always the same ground, always the same season — and settle disputes, arrange marriages, trade mammoths, and decide collectively what the coming year would ask of them.
It worked for thousands of years. It worked until the Molten Imperium began moving south.
Structure
Governance was oral and seasonal. The assembly’s decisions were binding but unwritten — they were remembered by the clan elders designated as memory-keepers, a role distinct from chieftain and considered more important. A chieftain could be replaced. A memory-keeper’s death was a catastrophe, because nothing they carried was written anywhere.
This is why almost nothing of the Confederation’s internal history survives. The memory-keepers died. The Imperium’s constructs did not distinguish between combatants and elders.
Thorall’s bloodline descends from a chieftain lineage, not a memory-keeper lineage. He carries the weight of leadership but not the weight of record. What he knows of the Confederation’s history is what his grandmother told him, which is what her grandmother told her, which grows thinner with each generation.
The Imperium’s Expansion
The Confederation first encountered Molten Imperium advance-constructs somewhere around 4,000–3,000 BCE — the dating is uncertain because the Confederation kept no dates. The early encounters were survivable. The constructs were clearing terrain for roads, not hunting people. The clans retreated south, which they had always done when the north became inhospitable. Retreating was not defeat. It was judgment.
The retreats became impossible to frame as judgment when the construct lines began advancing faster than the clans could move with their herds. Mammoths require grazing grounds. Grazing grounds are fixed. The Confederation’s military capacity — real, significant, built on mammoth cavalry and tundra warfare — was designed for raids and short conflicts. It was not designed for a sustained front against constructs that did not need to eat, sleep, or mourn their losses.
By roughly 2,000 BCE the Confederation’s formal assembly structure had collapsed. The clan representatives could no longer reach the meeting ground safely. What remained were isolated clan groups, moving independently, slowly losing contact with each other.
The Starfall and After
The Starfall struck the western continent’s interior, but its effects reached the far south through tremor, fragment-fall, and the collapse of the broader arcane network that had quietly been stabilizing weather patterns for centuries. The tundra fractured — literally — as Starfall shards fell into the ice. The terrain that the surviving clans depended on broke apart and refroze wrong.
Thorall’s group survived. Whether any other clan groups survived in isolation is unknown. Thorall does not know. He has been sending scouts south and east for thirty years. None have returned with news of other survivors, but none have returned with news of their absence either. He does not record this in the assembly decisions, because there is no assembly. He records it nowhere, because he has no memory-keeper.
The Confederation’s oral record ends somewhere in the chaos between the Imperium’s advance and the Starfall. What Thorall carries now is a memory of a memory of a memory — and the knowledge that this is the last generation in which even that survives, unless something changes.
Connections

Thorall — last known chieftain of the surviving remnant; carrier of the Confederation’s remaining oral history.
Frozen Fracture Tundras — the Confederation’s homeland.
Molten Imperium — the civilization whose expansion destroyed the Confederation’s formal structure.
The Great Shelf — the meeting ground where Thorall and Aaron negotiated the Treaty of the Melting World; also the site of one of the Confederation’s former seasonal assemblies, though Thorall has never said this to Aaron.

(He chose this location. He did not explain why.)
Compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.

Factions-and-Organisations/Pre-Starfall/.title: Verdant Dominion
Factions-and-Organisations/Pre-Starfall/.content:
The Verdant Dominion occupied the eastern coast of the eastern continent for approximately eight thousand years. It did not expand through conquest. It expanded through growth — literally. Its practitioners developed a form of magic that cultivated living borders: hedgerows that could not be cut, root-networks that redirected rivers, canopies that filtered light in ways that made agriculture within the Dominion uniquely productive and agriculture outside it subtly, persistently difficult.
Its neighbors found this deeply irritating and largely impossible to counter militarily, since there was nothing to fight. You cannot siege a forest that regrows overnight. You cannot starve a city whose walls are alive and bearing fruit.
The Molten Imperium, on the Dominion’s western flank, spent several centuries attempting various strategies before settling into a cold coexistence. They competed for influence over the smaller states between them — a quiet, grinding political conflict conducted through trade agreements and construct demonstrations rather than open war.
Magic and Doctrine
The Dominion’s magic was naturalistic in origin but highly sophisticated in practice by the civilization’s peak. Its practitioners — called Cultivators — did not command nature so much as negotiate with it: studying what a given ecosystem wanted to do and then arranging conditions to make that outcome serve human purposes. The philosophy was that magic was a conversation between the practitioner and the world, not a tool the practitioner wielded.
This is philosophically close to what Asterion taught about astral magic — that the sky does not answer those who try to rewrite its patterns, only those who learn to listen. Whether Asterion spent time in the Dominion, or the Dominion independently developed similar conclusions, is not recorded.
Lumia’s lineage traces to the Dominion, though how directly is unclear. Her approach to magic — preservation, guidance, tending rather than commanding — carries the Dominion’s signature.
Relationship with the Celestial Concord
The Dominion was among the earliest and most committed participants in the Celestial Concord, seeing in Asterion’s framework a formalization of conclusions it had already reached independently. Concord relay towers on the eastern coast were built with Dominion cooperation and maintained with Dominion labor for centuries.
When the Concord began militarizing in its later centuries, the Dominion grew uncomfortable and increasingly insular. It did not leave the Concord formally — it simply stopped attending.
Collapse
The Dominion did not fall in the Starfall impact directly — it fell in the hours and days afterward, when its practitioners died en masse trying to manage the shockwave through their living-border networks. The borders absorbed the damage as designed. The practitioners who were channeling those borders at the moment of impact did not survive the feedback.
Without practitioners to direct it, the living magic the Dominion had cultivated over eight thousand years had nowhere to go. It accelerated. It grew without instruction, without purpose, without the guiding hand that had always told it what shape to take. The result was the Verdant Rupture — the Dominion’s greatest achievement consuming its own ruins in a form that looks like life but moves like something that has forgotten why.
The Green Seat, the Dominion’s capital, is somewhere inside the Rupture. Nobody has found it. The Rupture does not encourage exploration near its center.
What Remains
The Verdant Wardens — a dispersed post-Starfall order operating in the Rupture — carry traces of Dominion methodology without knowing its name. They use a script for their records that no other culture recognizes, and they did not receive it from Lumia, who is the nearest living connection to the Dominion’s tradition. Where the script came from, they cannot say. They have always used it.
The thing that Lumia encountered in the Rupture — “that wasn’t an animal” — is more consistent with a Dominion-era cultivated organism that has been growing without direction for sixty years than with anything the Starfall introduced. This interpretation has not been formally proposed by anyone, because no one alive knows enough about the Dominion to propose it.
Connections

Verdant Rupture — the Dominion’s territory, transformed.
Lumia — carries the Dominion’s magical tradition, though the lineage is indirect.
The Celestial Concord — longtime partner institution; the Dominion was among its most genuine allies.
Molten Imperium — the Dominion’s rival for influence across the eastern continent’s interior.
The Verdant Wardens — a post-Starfall order operating within the Rupture, unknowingly carrying Dominion methodology.

Compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.

Items-and-Mechanics/Bonk.title: A mace and exosuit belonging to [[Bogrund]], treated as a companion
Items-and-Mechanics/Bonk.content:
Bonk is, depending on the moment, Bogrund’s weapon, his armor, and his closest companion — and he treats it as all three at once. As a weapon, Bonk toggles between a heavy melee mace and a ranged flail form. As armor, the same construct forms the suit Bogrund wears and can detach from, standing guard on its own while empowering nearby allies.
Bonk doesn’t speak, but Bogrund has no trouble understanding it anyway. When Starfall shards lit the horizon, it was Bonk who grew restless first — eager to march toward the crater and, in its own way, take a swing at whatever came out of it. Bogrund grumbled, tightened a few bolts, and went along anyway.
Connections

Bogrund — Bonk’s owner, partner, and closest friend.
Machine Wastes — where the two of them are usually found.

Note
This account is compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.

Items-and-Mechanics/Constellation-Lines-.filePath: Items and Mechanics/Constellation Lines & Star Points.md
Items-and-Mechanics/Constellation-Lines-.title: [[Asterion]]'s discipline for mapping [[Starfall Magic|the Pattern]] through the stars
Items-and-Mechanics/Constellation-Lines-.content:
Among the many ways mortals have learned to work with the Pattern, Asterion’s is among the oldest and most precise: astral cartography, the practice of reading the Pattern’s threads through the night sky.
A Star Point marks a place where the Pattern surfaces close enough to the world to be touched and used. Casting near one, or creating one through a working, anchors magic to that location — a fixed point the Pattern remembers. A Constellation Line connects two or more Star Points, channeling the Pattern’s influence along the line between them rather than at a single spot, with effects growing stronger wherever lines cross or converge.
This is the foundation of the magic Asterion wields, and of the maps he spent millennia drawing — not maps of geography, but of where the Pattern runs closest to the surface of the world.
Erased Constellations
Since the Starfall tore through the Pattern, constellations that Asterion once charted — and which later vanished entirely during the Age of Omens — have begun resurfacing in unexpected places. Not in the sky, but as echoes within certain individuals. Asterion has spent the post-Starfall era tracking these echoes, convinced each one is a fragment of a star-pattern that should no longer exist — and a clue toward The Cosmic Devourer he once warned the Concord about.
Connections

Asterion — originator and primary practitioner of this discipline.
Starfall Magic — the broader system this discipline draws on.
The Cosmic Devourer — the source of the erased constellations Asterion tracks.

Note
This account is compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.

Items-and-Mechanics/Resonance-Stones.title: Stones hauled by [[Thorall]]'s mammoths for [[Aaron]] during the Treaty of the Melting World
Items-and-Mechanics/Resonance-Stones.content:
When Thorall and Aaron struck their bargain on the Great Shelf, Thorall’s mammoths hauled a set of resonance-stones so that Aaron could draw the glaciers’ excess heat away rather than let it drown the Shoals or bury the tundra. What the stones actually are has never been fully explained — their ability to channel and redirect elemental energy on demand has led some to speculate they may be a refined or shaped form of Starfall fragment, though neither Thorall nor Aaron has confirmed this.
Connections

Thorall and Aaron — used the stones together during the Treaty of the Melting World.
Starfall Fragments — a possible, unconfirmed origin.

Note
This account is compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.

Items-and-Mechanics/Starfall-Fragments.title: Smaller fragments of the Starfall, distinct from [[The Eternis Core]]
Items-and-Mechanics/Starfall-Fragments.content:
Unlike The Eternis Core — a single, sentient fragment that chose its own vessel — most Starfall fragments are smaller, inert, and unpredictable. They began surfacing worldwide a few years after the Starfall, scattered through the Starfall Shard Zones and beyond.
Their effects vary wildly from fragment to fragment: some amplify the power of whoever wields them, some corrupt their bearer slowly, and some destabilize the land around them permanently, giving rise to the warped biomes found throughout the Shardfall Belts. As fragments were discovered, new factions and ideologies formed around their use — some treating them as weapons, some as energy sources, and some as objects of religious significance, the seeds of the world’s Fragment Cults.
Connections

The Eternis Core — a singular, sentient exception to how most fragments behave.
Starfall Shard Zones — where most fragments are found.
Fragment Cults — factions that formed around fragment use.

Note
This account is compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.

Items-and-Mechanics/Starfall-Magic.title: How magic is worked, and what it costs
Items-and-Mechanics/Starfall-Magic.content:
Physics in this world remains ordinary — gravity falls, fire climbs, time passes the way it always has. Magic doesn’t override these laws so much as negotiate with them, asking the world to bend for a moment rather than replacing how it works.
Underlying everything is an unseen order some call the Pattern — not written, not alive, but aware of being used. Most magic only touches its outer threads, which bend under a working and settle back into place once it’s done. Those who reach deeper are remembered by the world, and rarely kindly.
Magic responds best to clarity and restraint. A precise, narrowly-aimed intention meets little resistance; a grand or reckless one meets much more. This is why a focused effect tends to hold, and an overreaching one tends to backfire on whoever cast it.
Stress and Consequence
Magic used often or carelessly strains the Pattern, and that strain leaves marks: land that never fully heals, creatures born wrong, memories that won’t stay where they’re put, places where shadow lingers longer than it should. These aren’t curses in the traditional sense — they’re scars, the way flesh scars after a wound. Some heal. Some fester. Some never fade.
The Starfall as a Wound
The Starfall was the deepest such wound the Pattern has ever taken — a tear, not a strain. Starfall Fragments are pieces of that tear, still humming faintly with both power and consequence. Small fragments can be coaxed into tools or weapons; larger ones reshape the land around them, birthing new beasts and new dangers. The Eternis Core, the largest known fragment, goes further still — it doesn’t just lend power. It listens, and it chooses.
Connections

Starfall Fragments and The Eternis Core — physical remnants of the Pattern’s deepest wound.
Constellation Lines & Star Points — one discipline for reading and working with the Pattern.
The Cosmic Devourer — whatever reached deepest into the Pattern, long before the Starfall.

Note
This account is compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.

Items-and-Mechanics/The-Eternis-Core.title: A Starfall fragment buried beneath [[Ashenvale Pyrehold]], vessel-bound to [[Krysta]]
Items-and-Mechanics/The-Eternis-Core.content:
The Eternis Core entered the world as part of the Starfall, embedding itself deep beneath the volcanic region of Ashenvale Pyrehold. Its presence alters the local geology, unintentionally stabilizes the volcano above it, and emits a constant, low-level cosmic resonance. Unlike most Starfall Fragments, the Eternis Core is singular and sentient — see that page for how ordinary fragments behave.
Rhaegor could sense the Core through this resonance from early in the Shattered Age, but never knew its exact nature, its precise location, or that it had arrived with the Starfall at all. He came to believe it was a stabilizing force, and a potential safeguard against a second Starfall — which led him to build the Trial Chamber network beneath his volcano, convinced that completing the trials would let someone find and wield the Core.
The truth was simpler and stranger: the Eternis Core chooses its own vessel. The trials were never a key, only a filter. Around 10–15 AD, the Core chose Krysta, asserting partial control over her and becoming a second voice in her mind, one of order, preservation, and control, alongside her own voice and the corrupting whisper of Varesa.
Notable Figures

Krysta — chosen vessel of the Eternis Core.
Rhaegor — sensed the Core for decades without understanding it; built the Trial Chambers around a mistaken belief about its purpose.

Note
This account is compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.

Items-and-Mechanics/Tide-Crystals.title: Luminous crystals that stabilize the waters of [[Tiderest Shoals]]
Items-and-Mechanics/Tide-Crystals.content:
Tide-crystals are the luminous formations woven into the coral bridges and kelp banners of Tiderest Shoals, lighting the village and, more importantly, calming the water around it. Their glow is steady rather than flickering, and the waters nearest them run unnaturally smooth even when the rest of The Shattered Seas churns.
Their relationship to the floating formations of the nearby Crystal Reef is not fully understood — whether the reef feeds the village’s crystals, grew from them, or simply shares a common origin remains an open question for anyone living there.
Connections

Tiderest Shoals — where the crystals are set into the village itself.
Crystal Reef — a possibly related formation nearby.
Aaron — chieftain of the village these crystals stabilize.

Note
This account is compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.

Locations/Ashenvale-Pyrehold.title: Ashenvale Pyrehold
Locations/Ashenvale-Pyrehold.content:
A volcanic mountain range dominated by a single active volcano, Rhaegor’s Peak, west of the World Scar. Compared to the rest of the fractured world, Ashenvale feels stable — but it is a tense, coiled stability, like something waiting.
Lava rivers here run in unnaturally straight lines, a side effect of the cosmic resonance emitted by the Eternis Core buried deep within the mountain. The blackened forests surrounding the peak burn easily and regrow oddly fast, and the region experiences heat storms in place of rain.
The Eternis Core
The Eternis Core arrived as part of the Starfall, embedding itself deep beneath the volcano. Its presence alters the local geology, unintentionally stabilizes the volcano, and emits a constant, low-level cosmic resonance that Rhaegor can sense but never fully understood. He believed it to be a stabilizing force and a potential safeguard against a second Starfall — not knowing it arrived with the first.
The Trial Chamber Network
Within the volcano, Rhaegor constructed an extensive trial chamber system, intended to test resolve, balance, and endurance, ensuring only a worthy protector could reach the Core. He believed completing the trials would allow someone to find and wield the Eternis Core. In truth, the Core chooses its own vessel — the trials were never a key, only a filter.
The Village
A village near the volcano survived the Starfall thanks to Rhaegor’s indirect protection. Krysta grew up here, defending it from Starfall-born monsters from a very young age — behavior that earned her both admiration and resentment. It was here that Varesa first began her subtle corruption of Krysta, and where Rhaegor later revealed himself, believing Krysta’s proven protectiveness marked her as worthy of the trials.
Notable Figures

Rhaegor — the Lava Warden, guardian of the region and the Eternis Core.
Krysta — grew up in the village beneath Rhaegor’s Peak; chosen vessel of the Eternis Core.
Varesa — began corrupting Krysta here, posing as a friend.

Locations/Bogrund's-Workshop.title: Bogrund's Workshop
Locations/Bogrund's-Workshop.content:
Bogrund’s workshop sits at the edge of the Machine Wastes, identifiable from a distance by the steam, sparks, and occasional small explosion. Inside, Bonk is maintained, repaired, and occasionally bolted back together after one disagreement or another.
It was from here that Bogrund and Bonk set out toward The Starfall Crater when the shards first lit the horizon — Bonk eager to confront whatever might emerge, Bogrund grumbling but following anyway.
Connections

Bogrund — lives and works here.
Bonk — maintained here.
Machine Wastes — the workshop’s surroundings.

Locations/Celestial-Concord-HQ.title: Celestial Concord HQ
Locations/Celestial-Concord-HQ.content:
Also known as the Meridian Library, this complex served as the operational heart of the Celestial Concord — not merely an archive, but the seat from which the Concord’s astral relay network, enforcement divisions, and magical law were coordinated. Its high vaults housed the Concord’s most complete records of astral cartography, much of it the original work of Asterion.
While the Great Concord was the city, the Meridian Library was its decision-making core — the place where the Gilded Age’s arbitration rulings were issued, and where the judgment-focused and preservation-focused sects most directly clashed before their formal split. By the time of the Concord’s fall, it had become less a library than an administrative fortress.
Asterion was inside the Meridian Library’s high vaults, finishing a map of the Western Reach, when the Starfall struck. He described the moment gravity itself seemed to lose its resolve: ink lifted from his brush before the impact wave hit, and the Great Spire shattered into massive blocks that drifted upward into what would become the floating debris of The Starfall Crater. He survived by being near the building’s edge as it came apart, watching his life’s work ascend into the High Sky.
The Meridian Library’s foundations are now exposed at the edge of the World Scar. Serathiel maintains a vigil here, convinced that something moved in the fog near the foundations, unaligned with the vertical. Asterion has visited the site and considers her watch a vigil over a memory rather than an active threat, though he has not been able to convince her to stand down.
Notable Figures
